newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Investors worry that deal not a deal in Kazakhstan.
newsitem.headline: Investors worry that deal not a deal in Kazakhstan.

text.p: Foreign investors in Kazakhstan were left wondering on Monday if a deal is ever a deal in the former Soviet republic after the government changed its mind on a tender result to manage the country's power grid.
On Saturday Kazakhstan awarded a contract to Sweden's ABB Power Grid Consortium Ltd to manage the oil-rich state's power transmission lines for 25 years.
But the deal came less than a week after the Kazakhs said Britain's National Grid Group had the exclusive right to negotiate the contract.
"A deal is not a deal in Kazakhstan," said one Western lawyer based in Almaty who has witnessed many such "agreements".
A Western diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said he found few reasons to encourage buisnesses from his home country to invest in Kazakhstan.
"As a diplomat I'm supposed to be here to boost trade with this country," he said. "But sometimes I feel most of my time is spent warning people off."
Businessmen regularly complain of deep-rooted corruption.

Kazakhstan, which boasts large reserves of oil, gas and metals thrown across an area of steppe five times the size of France, is looking to a fire-sale of state assets in a hunt for cash to pay off a mountain of unpaid wages and pensions.

But while officials like to boast about the speed of the sell-off, unprecedented for a former Soviet republic, many determined investors have tripped at the last minute over the country's stop-go tender process.

In January, the government axed a framework deal with Germany's Deutsche Telekom AG who planned to take a 49 percent share in the republic's telecoms monopoly, NAK Kazakhtelekom. Another tender for the enterprise is near to a close.
Uncertainty also overhangs Argentina's Bridas Energy Corp's exclusive right to negotiate with the government on a 15-year contract to manage Kazakhstan's gas pipeline network.

Sarybai Kalmurzayev, director of the Kazakh finance ministry's state property department, said if Bridas failed to come up with a better offer this week, the government would start negotiating with Gaz de France.
"Our aim is to get more for Kazakhstan," Kalmurzayev said.
A Western businessman based in Almaty said the power grid tender was a good example of Kazakhstan's unpopular tender process.
"One party thinks they've got a deal and then things change at the last minute," he said. "From the point of view of foreign investors, the process isn't transparent, it's not helpful."
So why do foreign companies, with plenty of other emerging markets in which to invest their money, bother?
"The prices are cheap," said the lawyer. "And it also attracts a lot of capital which would be difficult to invest (legally) elsewhere," he said.
The businessman concurred. "In CIS countries and particularly Kazakhstan, the perception is that these assets are relatively undervalued," he said.
"There's now a real pressure from shareholders for the bigger returns from emerging markets and whoever gets in first usually gains."
